strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated taxonomy grounded in principled frameworks (scene graphs for composition, philosophical reasoning categories) rather than heuristic designs
High-complexity benchmark reflecting real-world scenarios with ~25 instances, ~20 attributes, ~15 relations per prompt, and multi-step one-to-many/many-to-one reasoning
Rigorous data construction and quality control: three different LRMs, human verification by 5 PhD students with 3+ revision rounds, cross-checking by ≥3 annotators with majority voting
Comprehensive evaluation of 27 models across three architectures with evaluation by multiple MLLMs (Gemini and Qwen) and human alignment study demonstrating robustness
Useful practical insights: composition is improving but reasoning remains the central bottleneck; MLLM-based encoders benefit T2I models
Strong reproducibility emphasis with detailed appendix, official API documentation, fixed random seeds, and promised code/data release
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and memorable motivation (title effectively captures composition vs. reasoning tradeoff)
weaknesses: Incomplete submission: Section 4 explicitly states 'fine-grained analyses and case studies are actively being conducted in progress and will be included in the next version'—key ablations and error analysis missing at review time

Evaluation validation gaps: human alignment study (Table 3) covers only 4 composition dimensions; all 8 reasoning dimensions lack human validation despite being core contributions. MLLM evaluators achieve only 81.1% balanced accuracy with humans

Questionable validity of some reasoning dimensions: Hypothetical Reasoning relies on detecting subtle visual details (perfect square wheels on all vehicles); Procedural Reasoning asks models to render only final state after 5 steps—intermediate steps not shown; Reconstructive Reasoning's 'most plausible cause' is inherently subjective

LRM-based data generation introduces systematic biases: all 1,080 prompts generated by LRMs; while three LRMs used, they share common characteristics. No analysis of whether benchmark is representative of real-world user prompts

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars in Table 2; no analysis of variance across 4 images per prompt; missing distribution analysis of dimension difficulty

Limited methodological novelty: scene graphs (Johnson et al. 2015), philosophical reasoning framework (Peirce 1934), and checklist-based MLLM evaluation (prior work by Hu et al. 2024) are established; contribution is primarily benchmark application rather than methodology

Incomplete human alignment validation: balanced accuracy metric used due to class imbalance suggesting possible success bias; unclear if benchmark is too easy; only ~100-200 sampled examples validated, not full benchmark

Interesting findings underexplored: BAGEL w/ Think results show composition drops (46.4→39.6) while reasoning improves (34.1→41.9) with intermediate thinking—phenomenon deserves deeper investigation but receives only surface discussion
Cost-driven evaluation choice: primary evaluator (Gemini 2.5 Flash) selected for cost but underperforms OpenAI o3 (81.1% vs 82.1%); results may not reflect true model capabilities

Limited generalization: only English prompts; evaluation only on synthetically-generated structured prompts, not naturally-phrased user prompts; missing analysis of real-world prompt distribution applicability

strengths: Comprehensive and principled 12-dimensional taxonomy grounded in scene graphs and philosophical reasoning frameworks
Rigorous data construction with multiple LRMs, human verification by 5 PhD students, and cross-checking across annotators
Substantial benchmark scale (1,080 prompts, ~13,500 checklist questions) with high compositional and reasoning complexity
Evaluation of 27 diverse T2I models across architectures and scales (21 open-source, 6 closed-source)
Clear presentation with effective examples demonstrating benchmark complexity
Human alignment study validating MLLM evaluation methodology (for composition dimensions)
weaknesses: Critical gap: Human alignment validation only covers 4 of 12 dimensions (composition only), leaving all 8 reasoning dimensions unvalidated—a major concern for a reasoning-focused benchmark
Evaluation methodology concern: 19% error rate in MLLM evaluation (Table 3 shows ~81% balanced accuracy) is non-trivial and undermines confidence in reported model scores
Fundamental conflation in reasoning evaluation: Checklist methodology measures outcome correctness but not whether the model actually performed multi-step reasoning as claimed
Paper explicitly incomplete: Acknowledges that 'fine-grained analyses and case studies are actively being conducted in progress'—critical analyses missing for top-tier submission
No ablation studies on checklist design, evaluation protocol validity, or prompt construction; no inter-question correlation analysis
Evaluation results raise methodological questions: suspiciously low text rendering scores and dramatic reasoning drops across all models lack adequate explanation
Limited human alignment scope: Single model (GPT-Image) used for validation; no inter-annotator agreement statistics; no breakdown by dimension or difficulty
Potential data bias: Using LRMs for both prompt and checklist generation could introduce correlated biases; no diversity analysis
Findings align with existing intuitions; limited actionable insights for model development; the 'thinking before generation' analysis shows mixed results without clear guidance
No statistical rigor: Missing confidence intervals, significance tests, error bars; no variance analysis across multiple generations; no benchmark correlation with existing benchmarks

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated 12-dimensional taxonomy addressing clear gaps in existing T2I benchmarks, grounded in scene graphs and philosophical reasoning frameworks
Significantly increased complexity compared to prior work: ~20-25 instances/attributes per prompt and multi-step reasoning chains that better reflect real-world scenarios
Rigorous data construction using 3 SOTA LRMs with extensive human verification across 5 expert annotators and 3 revision rounds
Effective checklist-based evaluation protocol with atomic yes/no questions enabling fine-grained and interpretable assessment
Large-scale evaluation across 27 diverse T2I models with clear, actionable insights (composition improving, reasoning remaining a critical bottleneck)
Strong reproducibility: official model sources documented, evaluation instructions detailed, multiple evaluators reported (Gemini 2.5 Flash + Qwen2.5-VL)
Clear presentation with excellent visualizations effectively communicating benchmark complexity and construction methodology
weaknesses: Insufficient analysis of MLLM evaluator reliability: Table 3 shows substantial variance (65.4%-82.6% balanced accuracy) across evaluators without sensitivity analysis of how this affects model rankings
Human alignment study lacks critical transparency: number of samples, annotator identity, inter-rater agreement statistics, and Spearman correlations between human and MLLM rankings are not reported

Data generation bias not adequately addressed: using LRMs may introduce circularity despite using 3 different LRMs (they share similar training corpora), with no rejection rate analysis or prompt bias examination

Missing critical ablations and analyses: no sensitivity to checklist design, limited error/failure case studies, and insufficient explanation for surprising results (e.g., why BAGEL w/ Think improves reasoning but hurts composition)

Questionable visual evaluability of complex reasoning tasks: some constraints (e.g., Logical Reasoning requiring inference of specific statements) may not be uniquely determined by visual evidence, risking ambiguous evaluation

Limited results analysis: despite comprehensive tables, analysis remains surface-level; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or investigation of why reasoning lags by 9.5-28.7 points
Modest per-dimension coverage (~90 prompts per dimension) and acknowledged limitations not addressed (English-only, sentence-level text rendering, no non-semantic aspects like aesthetics)
Paper acknowledges important experimental results are 'in progress'—these should be included for completeness

strengths: Comprehensive 12-dimensional taxonomy (4 composition + 8 reasoning) grounded in established frameworks (scene graphs, philosophical reasoning types) addressing clear gaps in prior work
Rigorous benchmark construction with multi-stage human verification (5 PhD annotators, 3+ review rounds), 3 LRMs to reduce bias, systematic filtering (feasibility, redundancy, refinement)
High-complexity prompts reflecting real-world scenarios: ~20 visual elements, ~170 tokens, multi-step reasoning (one-to-many, many-to-one), existential negation

Robust evaluation protocol: atomic yes/no questions for fine-grained assessment, MLLM evaluator (Gemini 2.5 Flash) validated against human judgment (81.1% balanced accuracy), open-source alternatives provided

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 38 models across architectures/scales, fine-grained analysis by complexity level (Table 6: 0-hop/1-hop/m-hop, POS/NEG, content/layout), actionable insights (reasoning bottleneck, encoder importance)

Valuable empirical findings: reasoning lags composition by 7-32+ points, native reasoning capability matters more than prompt rewriting, unified models show advantages, clear stepwise effect in logical reasoning complexity
Extensive transparency and reproducibility: detailed appendices with guidelines, fixed random seeds, promised public release of leaderboard/code/dataset, clear specification of all components
weaknesses: Limited scope reduces generalizability: T2I-only (no video/multimodal), English-only, object-centric (limited human/face scenarios), excludes non-semantic aspects (aesthetics, diversity). These design choices, while acknowledged, limit real-world applicability

MLLM evaluator concerns: primary evaluation uses closed-source Gemini 2.5 Flash (reproducibility risk), large variance between evaluators in Table 5 (65.4-88.4), no inter-rater agreement for human verification reported, always-'Yes' answer design may miss false positives

Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; no variance analysis across 3 LRM sources or 4 images per prompt; statistical comparison between model types missing

Benchmark design justification gaps: complexity targets (~25 instances) are aspirational, not post-hoc validated; limited ablation studies; negative instances underrepresented (1/5); dimension definitions sometimes loose/overlapping (GR vs AR both involve pattern transfer)

Limited failure mode analysis: mostly aggregate scores without systematic investigation of *why* models fail; fine-grained analysis only subset of dimensions; no error categorization or root-cause analysis; qualitative examples are anecdotal

Prompt rewriting section (Sec 4.3) feels tangential: uses different model (o3) for rewriting vs evaluation, insights are incremental ('textual reasoning insufficient'), limited exploration of multimodal reasoning mechanisms

Dataset artifact concerns: LRM-assisted construction may introduce systematic biases; no analysis of whether diversity is genuine or reflects LRM quirks; potential bias toward models trained on similar web data not discussed

strengths: Comprehensive 12-dimensional taxonomy jointly covering composition and reasoning with principled structure based on scene graphs and philosophical frameworks
Rigorous benchmark construction with 1,080 prompts, 13,500 questions, human verification by 5 PhD students, and multi-stage filtering using 3 LRMs to reduce bias
Large-scale evaluation of 38 T2I models across diverse architectures providing substantial empirical evidence
Fine-grained checklist-based evaluation methodology enabling precise error attribution better than existing metrics like CLIPScore
Clear and actionable empirical findings: reasoning is the primary bottleneck, composition steadily improving, insights on prompt rewriting effectiveness (Table 4)
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices documenting construction guidelines, evaluation instructions, and experimental details
Well-presented paper with clear visualizations and comprehensive results tables
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily packages existing concepts (scene graphs from Johnson et al. 2015, philosophical reasoning framework, checklist-based VQA evaluation from prior work) with insufficient methodological or theoretical contribution
Incomplete human alignment study: only covers 4/12 dimensions (composition only), missing validation for 8 reasoning dimensions; no inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's κ) for human annotators

MLLM evaluator concerns: heavy reliance on Gemini 2.5 Flash creates systematic bias risk; substantial performance variance across LLMs (65.4-81.1% on same tasks); binary yes/no scoring ignores partial correctness and visual ambiguity

LRM-generated prompts with arbitrary complexity numbers (~25 instances, ~20 attributes) may have systematic biases; limited coverage (English-only, primarily objects/animals, single-image generation) without diversity analysis

Overly simplistic evaluation: ratio-based scoring (25/33) ignores error severity, aesthetics, and realism; text rendering evaluated at sentence-level only; no confidence intervals or significance testing

Limited analysis depth: does not explain WHY reasoning is hard or investigate underlying causes; no ablation on whether all 12 dimensions are necessary; missing correlation analysis between composition and reasoning; prompt rewriting shows textual reasoning insufficient but alternatives unexplored

Experimental design issues: prompt rewriting uses OpenAI o3 (not in main evaluation set); arbitrary dimension selection without boundary justification (e.g., BR vs HR); unclear generalization to other T2I applications; benchmark created at fixed time amid rapid model evolution

Questionable significance for top-tier venue: findings are largely confirmatory (reasoning bottleneck is unsurprising); limited guidance for model improvement; unclear if benchmark captures user needs; reads as dataset paper rather than research contribution

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark addressing clear gap: first to jointly evaluate composition and reasoning capabilities across 12 well-motivated dimensions grounded in scene graphs and philosophical frameworks
High-quality dataset construction with rigorous human verification (5 PhD students, 3 rounds), use of multiple LRMs to reduce bias, and documented guidelines
Thorough evaluation of 38 T2I models across diverse architectures with human alignment validation for composition dimensions and extensive fine-grained analysis
Strong methodology with atomic checklist design, careful MLLM instructions emphasizing visual evidence, and multiple-image robustness checks
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices, documented model sources, promised code/benchmark/leaderboard release
Insightful findings revealed through fine-grained analysis (negative vs positive constraints, hop-level progression, variant vs invariant patterns)
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations, comprehensive examples, and clear communication
weaknesses: MLLM evaluation limitations: human alignment validation only on 4/12 dimensions; reasoning dimensions lack human verification; substantial MLLM variance (Table 5, ~10% range); potential hallucination in checklist answering not discussed
Scope limitations: English-only, limited human/face content, static images only, no aesthetic/realism/diversity metrics, specific complexity numbers may not reflect real-world variation
Statistical rigor gaps: no confidence intervals or significance testing, no inter-rater agreement metrics provided, variance across 4 images per prompt not analyzed
Dataset design: LRM-generated prompts filtered from 300→90 per dimension (70% reduction); potential systematic biases in LRM behavior not fully addressed; sentence-level text evaluation

Reasoning evaluation concerns: some dimensions feel ad-hoc (why 8 specific reasoning types?); checklist-based evaluation may miss implicit understanding; Section 4.3 shows textual reasoning insufficient but architectural implications underexplored
Limited methodological novelty: primarily a benchmark paper; findings somewhat expected (composition improving, reasoning harder); prompt rewriting analysis somewhat tangential
Potential for near-term saturation: top models at 77-85% overall, may reach ceiling as models improve despite reasoning differentiation
